title: MSEP Area 2025 Data Summaries
text:
Introduction
This website is a collection of documents summarizing the condition of the Mississippi Sound and its watershed in 2025, as compared to “baseline” conditions (which we also need to define, at appropriate spatial scales for each parameter). This will be the technical supporting information for what ultimately goes into a State of the Sound report. The State of the Sound will be public-facing, whereas the intended audience for this document is largely technical.
The outputs are compiled as a ‘quarto book’. Each chapter is produced by a separate .qmd file.
The purpose of the book format is to make the outputs readily findable and accessible. It also serves as an outline for future undertakings like a complete baseline characterization of these parameters and future State of the Sound reports.
You can download a pdf version of this entire book by clicking on the pdf icon on the right side of the toolbar at the top of this page.

title: 1  Precipitation
text:
1.1 Overall Summary
2025 was normal-to-dry across the MSEP watershed, with annual total precipitation within 5% of the 30-year average in 4 of the 14 subbasins, and 10-18% lower than normal in the other 8 subbasins. See Figure 1.5 and Figure 1.3 in particular.

title: 1  Precipitation
text:
1.2 Supporting Information

1.2.1 Annual Totals, Averaged to HUC8
Annual totals were calculated from monthly precipitation data obtained from the PRISM Group at Oregon State University, https://prism.oregonstate.edu which were accessed 29 July 2026.

1.2.1.1 Map









Figure 1.1: Map of annual precipitation total (inches), averaged to the HUC-8 (subbasin) level.






1.2.1.2 Time Series Graph
How does 2025 compare to past years? This graph uses data compiled in the msepBaselineData package.








Figure 1.2: Time series of annual precipitation total (inches) by HUC-8 (subbasin). Each line represents a subbasin.








1.2.2 Annual Anomalies
Because the climate normal on the coast is upwards of 60 inches, and it looks like the coast was in the mid-50s range in 2025, which is a little drier than normal. Climate normals in the northern part of the watershed are in the mid-to-upper 50s so they look about typical for 2025. I’m eyeballing here and the color scale is slightly different, but see the MSEP Characterization chapter on precipitation for the details I have compiled in the past (climate normals from NCEI).

1.2.2.1 Map









Figure 1.3: Map of 2025 differences from 30-year average precipitation, in inches, averaged to the HUC-8 (subbasin) level. Darker colors indicate totals further from the long-term average.






1.2.2.2 Time Series Graph








Figure 1.4: Time series of annual anomalies (difference between that year and the 30-year climate normal, in inches) by HUC-8 (subbasin). Each line represents a subbasin.





The y-axis may not be that meaningful if you don’t already know that the annual normal amount is around 60 inches. So let’s look at the difference as a percent.
From this 20-year time series, we can see that generally things tend to be similar (compared to normal) across all the HUC8s in the watershed. Some years have more variability, like 2019 and 2020. We had a fairly long stretch from 2012-2021 or so where it generally was normal to wetter-than-normal. 2025 was generally drier than normal across the watershed; drier in some HUC8s than others. As seen from the map, the southern counties were the ones that generally were much drier than normal.


1.2.2.3 Interactive time series








Figure 1.5: Time series of differences from 30-year average precipitation, by HUC-8 (subbasin). Each line represents a subbasin. In the HTML version of this document, hovering over a line shows which subbasin it represents, and hovering over a point shows the precipitation total and anomaly for that year in the subbasin.







1.2.3 Monthly Totals
Monthly data are from the PRISM Group at Oregon State University, https://prism.oregonstate.edu and were accessed 29 July 2026. They are again averaged to HUC8.








Figure 1.6: Map of monthly precipitation totals (inches), averaged to the HUC-8 (subbasin) level.





May seems to have been the wettest month in 2025, and that’s not really typical - actually in the climate normals (see them here), the color scale only goes up to 8.5 inches per month, and May 2025 exceeded that.


1.2.4 Monthly Anomalies
From long-term climate normals, as provided by the PRISM Climate Group at Oregon State University and processed into the msepBaselineData package’s precip_normals_huc8avg dataset.








Figure 1.7: Map of monthly precipitation anomalies (difference from 30-year climate normals, in inches), averaged to the HUC-8 (subbasin) level.

title: 10  Beach Advisories
text:
10.2 Supporting Information

10.2.1 DEQ Beach Sampling
Make a map where each station is represented by a point, and the point size is based on the number of days that station was under advisory in the year.
no. of beach closure days by station (see PPBEP’s online map)

Can download advisory/closure info from DEQ: https://beaches.mdeq.ms.gov/Historical/HCA
Per station, calculate # advisories/closures, # days under advisory/closure (total), mean or median # days per advisory/closure
Aggregate across coast: how many days under advisory/closure across all stations (sum of station totals); break down whether it’s just a few troublesome sites (seems to be based on presentations I’ve seen from DEQ) and what % of advisory/closure days came from those few sites
